title.en: Local transform, unit, axis, origin and pivot handoff

summary: Freeze one coordinate conversion and encode working pivots through node hierarchy so imported local transforms remain decomposable, measurable and animation-ready.
objective: The loaded asset has correct metre scale, orientation, hierarchy and hinge centers without compensating root transforms or double-applied rotations.
applies_when: A Blender asset with meaningful origins, parents, non-uniform scale, hinges or animated parts is delivered through glTF to Three.js.
example_prompts: Export a Blender cabinet whose doors pivot on their hinges and measure correctly in metres in Three.js.
Debug a nested GLB that is upright only after a compensating root rotation.
negative_signals: Apply axis conversion in both exporter and loader
Bake a moving pivot by repeatedly rewriting vertex positions
not_for: Geospatial coordinate precision at planetary scales.
Physics center-of-mass selection, which can differ from the visual pivot.

principles: A node transform is local to its parent; world pose is the composed hierarchy. Diagnose the first incorrect local transform instead of adding a compensating world transform at the root.
glTF fixes right-handed axes and metres. Convert once at export and keep application coordinates consistent with the loaded asset.

A working pivot is represented robustly by hierarchy: place a pivot parent at the hinge and offset the visible mesh child. This survives formats that carry node transforms but no authoring-tool origin workflow.
implementation: Set Blender scene units and model dimensions explicitly. Apply scale where geometry operations require stable object-space widths, then recheck dimensions; preserve intended object rotations/translations and parent inverses.

For each articulated part, create a parent node or Empty at the hinge/pivot and offset the mesh child relative to it. Name the pivot semantically and animate the pivot node, not displaced mesh vertices.

Export with Y Up as the single Blender-to-glTF conversion. Avoid flattening hierarchy when semantic pivots are required; if a node matrix is non-decomposable and must animate, remodel it as decomposable translation, quaternion rotation and scale nodes.
Load with GLTFLoader. In Three.js, keep imported local position/quaternion/scale and inspect matrixWorld after hierarchy update. Application controls own changes to the named pivot node.
Include a one-metre calibration bar, asymmetric +X/+Z markers and a hinged panel. Compare local TRS, world endpoints and hinge position numerically after import.
observable_checks: The calibration bar measures 1.0 in runtime units and axis markers face the declared directions with no compensating root rotation.
Rotating the pivot parent keeps the hinge point fixed while the mesh child follows the expected arc.
Reparenting or updating the hierarchy produces the predicted matrixWorld; local transforms remain decomposable and finite.

creative_affordances: One visual mesh can sit under several semantic transform nodes when controls need staged motion.
A visible axis/pivot debug layer can become part of an educational inspection mode.
known_limits: Visual pivot, physics center of mass and manipulation handle may be different application concepts.
This contract covers local-scale scenes, not floating-origin geospatial systems.
Authored reusable guidance; no export, import or runtime artifact was executed for this record.

claims.statement: glTF 2.0 uses a right-handed coordinate system with positive Y up, positive Z forward and metres for linear distances; a node has either a matrix or translation, rotation and scale properties, animated nodes target TRS rather than matrix, and local transforms compose in translation-rotation-scale order. Blender's exporter offers Y Up conversion, while Three.js Object3D exposes local transforms and a composed matrixWorld.
claims.scope: glTF 2.0 coordinate and node semantics plus documented Blender 4.5 and current Three.js APIs; pivot hierarchy design is authored guidance.
